The nozzle arrangement is connected to a source of pressurized fluid and is configured to produce rapid pulsed discharges of that fluid in quick succession. In operation, pressurized fluid is supplied to the nozzle arrangement and is released intermittently, so that the discharge occurs as a series of short, high-speed pulses rather than as a continuous stream.

The nozzle body includes an inlet through which the pressurized fluid enters. The inlet feeds the fluid into an internal chamber formed within the nozzle body. At the downstream end of this chamber, a wall is provided with an outlet hole through which the fluid can be discharged from the nozzle.

A prodder is positioned so that it can move within the outlet hole. The prodder is movable between a sealed position and an unsealed position. In the sealed position, the prodder closes or blocks the outlet hole, preventing fluid from escaping. In the unsealed position, the prodder permits the pressurized fluid in the chamber to pass through the outlet hole, thereby producing a discharge pulse.

Upstream of the prodder is a sprung plunger that is connected to the prodder so that movement of the plunger controls movement of the prodder. The plunger includes an annular seal that engages with the surrounding wall of the chamber. This annular seal acts as a movable chamber wall, allowing the effective volume of the chamber to change as the plunger moves.

During operation, pressurized fluid enters the chamber through the inlet. As the chamber fills, the fluid pressure acts on the plunger and causes it to move upstream against the force of its spring. This movement is transmitted to the prodder, causing the prodder to move from its sealed position toward an unsealed position. Once the outlet hole is opened, fluid is rapidly discharged from the chamber through the outlet hole.

As the fluid is discharged, the pressure within the chamber falls. The spring then urges the plunger back downstream, moving the prodder back into its sealed position so that the outlet hole is closed again. The chamber can then refill with pressurized fluid, repeating the cycle. In this way, the combined action of the pressurized fluid, the sprung plunger, and the movable prodder produces rapid, successive pulsed discharges from the nozzle.

A nozzle arrangement for generating rapid pulsed discharges of pressurized fluid includes a housing defining a chamber that receives fluid under pressure from a supply. The chamber communicates with an outlet hole through which the fluid is discharged in pulses. A movable prodder is positioned so that it can cooperate with a sprung, sealed plunger to control the opening and closing of the outlet hole.

In use, pressurized fluid enters the chamber and causes the internal pressure to rise. As the chamber fills, the pressure acts on the sealed plunger, urging it against the force of its spring. This movement shifts the plunger and the associated prodder from their normal sealing position. When the plunger has moved far enough, the prodder unseats or releases the seal at the outlet hole, allowing the pressurized fluid in the chamber to escape rapidly through the outlet.

The sudden discharge reduces the pressure in the chamber. As the pressure falls, the spring returns the plunger toward its original position. The prodder is moved back with it, causing the outlet hole to be sealed again. Once resealed, the chamber can refill with pressurized fluid, and the same sequence repeats.

By using the interaction between the filling chamber, movable prodder, spring-loaded sealed plunger, and outlet hole, the nozzle arrangement automatically alternates between a charging state and a discharge state. This makes it possible to produce repeated, rapid pulses of fluid in quick succession without requiring a separate external actuator for each pulse. The arrangement is therefore suitable for applications where short, high-speed bursts of fluid are required, such as pulsed spraying, cleaning, cutting, atomizing, or other controlled fluid-delivery processes.
outputs.L5:
A nozzle arrangement is an essential component in many fluid, gas, and spray systems. It is designed to control the direction, speed, shape, and distribution of a discharged medium. Depending on the application, a nozzle arrangement may be used to deliver water, air, fuel, steam, chemicals, or other fluids with a high degree of precision.

A typical nozzle arrangement includes one or more nozzles connected to a supply line or manifold. The nozzles may be fixed, adjustable, or rotatable, allowing the flow pattern to be adapted to specific operating conditions. In some systems, multiple nozzles are arranged in a row, circle, or other geometric pattern to ensure uniform coverage over a target area. This is common in irrigation systems, industrial cleaning devices, cooling systems, combustion equipment, and spray coating installations.

The design of a nozzle arrangement can significantly affect system performance. Important factors include nozzle diameter, outlet shape, spray angle, pressure level, flow rate, and material selection. For example, a narrow nozzle opening may produce a high-velocity jet, while a wider or specially shaped outlet may create a fine mist or fan-shaped spray. Materials such as stainless steel, brass, ceramics, or high-strength plastics are often selected based on resistance to pressure, temperature, corrosion, and wear.

In advanced applications, a nozzle arrangement may include control features such as valves, sensors, or actuators. These allow automatic adjustment of the flow rate, spray direction, or operating pressure. Such arrangements can improve efficiency, reduce waste, and provide more accurate process control.

Overall, a nozzle arrangement plays a critical role in directing and managing fluid flow. By selecting the appropriate nozzle type and configuration, it is possible to improve performance, reliability, and energy efficiency in a wide range of technical and industrial systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style description of a nozzle arrangement connected to a pressurized fluid source that produces rapid pulsed discharges through an outlet hole.
counterfactuals.output:
**Title:** Nozzle Arrangement for Generating Rapid Pulsed Fluid Discharges

**Abstract**  
A nozzle arrangement is provided for connection to a pressurized fluid source and configured to emit a sequence of rapid pulsed discharges through an outlet hole. The arrangement includes a nozzle body defining an internal fluid passage, an inlet configured to receive pressurized fluid, and an outlet aperture through which the fluid is discharged. A flow-interrupting member is disposed within the nozzle body and is movable between a first position permitting fluid communication with the outlet aperture and a second position restricting or interrupting such communication. An actuator or pressure-responsive mechanism cyclically drives or permits movement of the flow-interrupting member to produce discrete pulses of fluid at the outlet. The arrangement may include a biasing element, timing chamber, valve seat, resonant element, or control passage to regulate pulse frequency, pulse duration, and discharge volume.

---

## Patent-Style Description

### Field of the Invention  
The present disclosure relates generally to fluid discharge devices and, more particularly, to a nozzle arrangement adapted to be connected to a pressurized fluid source and to produce rapid, repeated pulsed discharges of fluid through an outlet opening.

### Background  
Nozzles connected to pressurized fluid supplies are commonly used to deliver a continuous stream or spray of liquid or gas. In certain applications, however, it is desirable to deliver the fluid in discrete pulses rather than as a substantially continuous flow. Pulsed discharge can improve distribution, reduce total fluid consumption, provide controlled impact, enhance atomization, or produce a desired cyclic flow pattern. Existing arrangements may require complex external valves, electronic controllers, or bulky mechanical assemblies. Accordingly, there is a need for a compact nozzle arrangement capable of producing rapid pulsed discharges using pressure from the fluid source and/or a simplified actuation mechanism.

### Summary  
In one embodiment, a nozzle arrangement includes a nozzle body having an inlet connectable to a pressurized fluid source, an internal chamber, and an outlet hole. A valve element is positioned between the inlet and the outlet hole and is configured to alternately open and close a flow path to the outlet hole. The valve element may be biased toward one position by a spring or resilient member and moved toward another position by fluid pressure, by a pressure differential, or by an actuator.

In another embodiment, the nozzle arrangement includes a pressure-responsive pulse generator in which pressurized fluid accumulates in a control chamber until a threshold pressure is reached. Upon reaching the threshold pressure, the valve element moves rapidly to an open position, allowing a burst of fluid to discharge through the outlet hole. The resulting pressure drop permits the valve element to return to a closed or restricted position, after which the cycle repeats.

In still another embodiment, the nozzle arrangement includes a reciprocating member, diaphragm, reed, poppet, spool, or shutter element arranged to periodically interrupt the flow through the outlet hole. The reciprocating member may be driven by the fluid itself, by a mechanical oscillator, by electromagnetic actuation, by piezoelectric actuation, or by pneumatic or hydraulic control pressure.

### Detailed Description  

A nozzle arrangement according to the present disclosure comprises a nozzle body formed from metal, polymer, ceramic, composite material, or any other material suitable for the intended operating pressure and fluid. The nozzle body includes an inlet port configured for threaded, flanged, push-fit, quick-connect, welded, or otherwise sealed connection to a pressurized fluid source. The pressurized fluid source may supply a liquid, gas, foamable medium, slurry, or multiphase fluid.

The nozzle body defines an internal flow passage extending from the inlet port toward an outlet hole. The outlet hole may be circular, elliptical, slot-shaped, annular, or otherwise shaped to produce a desired discharge pattern. The outlet hole may be formed directly in the nozzle body or in a replaceable nozzle insert secured to the nozzle body. The insert may include a converging section, diverging section, straight bore, swirl chamber, or atomizing feature.

A valve seat is disposed upstream of the outlet hole. A flow-interrupting member cooperates with the valve seat to control fluid flow to the outlet hole. The flow-interrupting member may comprise a poppet, ball, diaphragm, spool, sliding sleeve, rotary disk, oscillating reed, flexible flap, or other member capable of cyclically varying the effective flow area. In a closed or restricted state, the member substantially prevents or reduces discharge through the outlet hole. In an open state, the member permits fluid to pass through the outlet hole as a pulse.

In one form, the flow-interrupting member is a poppet valve biased toward the valve seat by a spring. Pressurized fluid is admitted to a chamber upstream of the poppet. When pressure acting on an effective surface of the poppet exceeds the spring force and any opposing pressure forces, the poppet lifts from the valve seat, allowing fluid to discharge through the outlet hole. The discharge reduces pressure in the chamber, whereupon the spring returns the poppet to the seat. Repetition of this pressure build-up and release produces rapid pulsed discharges.

A control chamber may be provided to influence timing of the pulsing cycle. The control chamber may communicate with the inlet through a restricted orifice, capillary passage, porous element, adjustable needle valve, or other flow restrictor. By controlling the rate at which the control chamber fills or vents, the frequency and duration of the pulses can be adjusted. An adjustment member may be provided to vary the restriction, spring preload, valve stroke, or outlet area.

In another form, the nozzle arrangement includes a diaphragm separating a pressure chamber from a control chamber. The diaphragm carries or actuates a valve closure element. Fluid pressure on one side of the diaphragm causes movement of the valve closure element relative to the outlet flow path. A vent or bleed passage causes periodic pressure equalization or pressure collapse, resulting in cyclic diaphragm movement and pulsed discharge.

In a further embodiment, a rotating or oscillating shutter is disposed adjacent the outlet hole. The shutter includes one or more openings that periodically align with the outlet hole to permit discharge. Rotation may be caused by a turbine or impeller located in the internal passage and driven by the pressurized fluid. As the shutter rotates, the outlet hole is alternately exposed and blocked, producing a train of fluid pulses. The pulse frequency may be determined by fluid flow rate, number of shutter openings, gearing ratio, or adjustable drag.

The nozzle arrangement may include a swirl-inducing structure upstream of the outlet hole. Such a structure may comprise tangential inlet passages, helical vanes, grooves, or a vortex chamber. The swirl-inducing structure may improve atomization, widen the spray pattern, or stabilize the pulsed discharge.

The outlet hole may be positioned at a distal end of the nozzle body and may have a diameter selected according to desired flow rate, discharge velocity, pressure drop, and pulse characteristics. Multiple outlet holes may be provided, each receiving pulsed flow from a common pulsing chamber or from separate pulsing mechanisms. The outlet holes may be arranged in a linear array, circular pattern, fan pattern, or other configuration.

The nozzle arrangement may further include a damping feature to limit impact or rebound of the flow-interrupting member. The damping feature may comprise an elastomeric stop, dashpot chamber, fluid cushion, magnetic damper, or resilient seat. Such damping can reduce wear, noise, and variation in pulse timing.

In some embodiments, an actuator is coupled to the flow-interrupting member. The actuator may be an electromagnetic solenoid, piezoelectric stack, magnetostrictive element, pneumatic piston, hydraulic piston, cam follower, or motor-driven mechanism. A controller may supply drive signals to the actuator to produce pulses having selected frequency, duty cycle, amplitude, or pulse sequence. A pressure sensor, flow sensor, position sensor, or acoustic sensor may provide feedback to the controller.

The nozzle arrangement may be configured to operate in a self-oscillating mode without external electrical control. In such an embodiment, the geometry of the internal passages, the mass of the movable member, the biasing force, and the compressibility or compliance of the fluid volume are selected so that fluid pressure causes repeated opening and closing of the flow path. The resulting pulsed discharge may occur at a frequency determined by the pressure of the fluid source, the volume of the chamber, the effective valve area, and the flow restriction characteristics.

Sealing elements may be provided between components of the nozzle body. Such sealing elements may include O-rings, gaskets, metal seals, lip seals, or molded resilient members. The nozzle body may be assembled from multiple parts to permit cleaning, replacement of the outlet insert, adjustment of the pulse mechanism, or substitution of springs and valve elements.

### Operation  
In operation, the inlet port is connected to a pressurized fluid source. Fluid enters the internal passage and is directed toward the pulsing mechanism. In an initial state, the flow-interrupting member restricts flow to the outlet hole. Pressure builds in an upstream chamber or control chamber until a force imbalance moves the flow-interrupting member away from its restricting position. Fluid then discharges rapidly through the outlet hole as a pulse. The discharge causes a pressure reduction or other restoring condition that returns the flow-interrupting member to its restricting position. The cycle repeats, thereby producing a rapid series of pulsed discharges.

The pulse frequency may be increased by reducing the chamber volume, reducing movable mass, increasing inlet pressure, decreasing valve stroke, or increasing the rate at which the control chamber is replenished or vented. The pulse duration may be adjusted by changing the valve stroke, spring force, outlet hole area, control passage size, or actuator timing.

### Advantages  
The disclosed nozzle arrangement can provide one or more of the following advantages:

1. generation of rapid fluid pulses from a pressurized fluid source;  
2. compact integration of the pulsing function within the nozzle body;  
3. reduced need for external valves or large control systems;  
4. adjustable pulse frequency, pulse width, and discharge volume;  
5. compatibility with liquids, gases, and multiphase fluids;  
6. improved atomization or distribution compared with continuous discharge; and  
7. replaceable outlet inserts for tailoring discharge characteristics.

### Exemplary Claims  

1. **A nozzle arrangement** comprising:  
   a nozzle body having an inlet configured for connection to a pressurized fluid source;  
   an internal chamber in fluid communication with the inlet;  
   an outlet hole configured to discharge fluid from the nozzle body; and  
   a flow-interrupting member disposed between the inlet and the outlet hole, the flow-interrupting member being movable between a first position in which fluid flow to the outlet hole is restricted and a second position in which fluid flow to the outlet hole is permitted;  
   wherein the flow-interrupting member is configured to move cyclically between the first and second positions to produce rapid pulsed discharges through the outlet hole.

2. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, further comprising a biasing member urging the flow-interrupting member toward the first position.

3. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, wherein the flow-interrupting member is pressure-responsive and is moved toward the second position when pressure within the internal chamber exceeds a threshold pressure.

4. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, further comprising a control chamber communicating with the inlet through a restricted passage, the control chamber being arranged to regulate a pulse frequency of the pulsed discharges.

5. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 4**, wherein the restricted passage includes an adjustable restriction.

6. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, wherein the flow-interrupting member comprises a poppet valve cooperating with a valve seat.

7. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, wherein the flow-interrupting member comprises a diaphragm coupled to a valve closure element.

8. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, wherein the flow-interrupting member comprises a rotating shutter having at least one opening that periodically aligns with the outlet hole.

9. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 8**, further comprising a fluid-driven impeller coupled to the rotating shutter.

10. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, further comprising an actuator coupled to the flow-interrupting member and configured to drive the flow-interrupting member cyclically.

11. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 10**, wherein the actuator comprises at least one of an electromagnetic actuator, a piezoelectric actuator, a pneumatic actuator, or a hydraulic actuator.

12. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, wherein the outlet hole is provided in a replaceable nozzle insert.

13. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, further comprising a swirl-inducing structure upstream of the outlet hole.

14. **The nozzle arrangement of claim 1**, wherein the nozzle body includes a plurality of outlet holes configured to receive pulsed fluid flow.

15. **A method of producing pulsed fluid discharge**, comprising:  
   supplying pressurized fluid to an inlet of a nozzle body;  
   accumulating fluid pressure in an internal chamber of the nozzle body;  
   moving a flow-interrupting member from a restricting position to an open position when a threshold condition is reached;  
   discharging a pulse of fluid through an outlet hole; and  
   returning the flow-interrupting member to the restricting position after discharge of the pulse, thereby enabling repeated pulsed discharges.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in formal patent language, a pressurized-fluid nozzle that repeatedly fills a chamber, opens an outlet with a prodder, discharges fluid, and reseals using a spring plunger mechanism.
counterfactuals.output:
A pressurized-fluid nozzle assembly comprises a nozzle body defining an internal charging chamber in fluid communication with a pressurized-fluid inlet and selectively in communication with an outlet orifice. A reciprocable plunger is disposed within the nozzle body and is biased by a spring toward a sealing position in which the plunger closes the outlet orifice and permits the charging chamber to be filled with pressurized fluid from the inlet.

The nozzle assembly further includes an actuating member, such as a prodder, probe, pin, or striker element, arranged to engage the plunger directly or indirectly. Upon engagement, the actuating member displaces the plunger against the force of the spring from the sealing position to an open position. In the open position, the outlet orifice is uncovered or otherwise placed in fluid communication with the charging chamber, thereby permitting the pressurized fluid accumulated within the chamber to be discharged through the outlet orifice.

After discharge, withdrawal or release of the actuating member permits the spring to return the plunger to the sealing position. The plunger thereby reseals the outlet orifice and re-establishes a closed charging volume within the chamber. Pressurized fluid supplied through the inlet subsequently refills the chamber, whereby the nozzle assembly is automatically conditioned for a subsequent discharge cycle. Repeated actuation of the prodder accordingly produces successive cycles of chamber filling, outlet opening, pressurized-fluid discharge, and spring-assisted resealing.

In one embodiment, the plunger includes a sealing face, valve head, or elastomeric sealing element configured to seat against a valve seat surrounding the outlet orifice. The spring may be a compression spring positioned between the plunger and an internal shoulder or end wall of the nozzle body, urging the sealing face into engagement with the valve seat. The inlet may include a check valve, restriction, or metering passage to regulate refilling of the chamber while preventing undesirable backflow during discharge.

In operation, pressurized fluid enters the chamber while the plunger is seated. The chamber remains charged until the prodder is advanced into engagement with the plunger. Movement of the prodder unseats the plunger, opening the outlet and allowing the fluid charge to exhaust through the nozzle. Upon retraction of the prodder, the spring advances the plunger back into sealing engagement with the outlet seat, terminating flow and allowing the chamber to refill. The assembly thereby provides a repeatable pulsed-discharge nozzle actuated by mechanical displacement of a spring-biased sealing plunger.
